# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Log Analytics and Microsoft Sentinel all use the same query language: Kusto Query Language (KQL). A KQL query is a pipeline — a table name followed by operators separated by "\|", each one working on the output of the previous one. Application Insights stores every incoming call in the requests table, every outgoing call in dependencies and every error in exceptions; all rows of one user action share one operation\_Id.  
In this lab you create your own Application Insights resource, send one hour of telemetry from the shop API with a script in Cloud Shell, filter and shape it with where, project and extend, aggregate it with summarize and bin(), visualise it with render, find the top failing dependencies, and use join and operation\_Id to connect failed requests to the dependency calls and exceptions that caused them. At the end you find the same incident again in the Failures blade, the Application map and the End-to-end transaction view.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can answer "which downstream call is failing and which users does it affect" in Application Insights with the portal and your own KQL. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You separate expected failures (404 for unknown products) from the real incident (the payment provider). |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your queries can be pinned to an Azure dashboard or used as log alert rules. |

You then investigate it with KQL in Application Insights → Logs and with the Failures, Application map and End-to-end transaction views. The hour ends 10 minutes before you run the script; the incident is minutes 20–35 of that hour. |
|  |
| YOUR MISSION: Create the resource, send the data, find and rank the failing dependencies, correlate them with requests and exceptions, and describe the incident with evidence. You have 35 minutes for the core tasks. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Application Insights writes three main tables. One user action is one operation: its operation\_Id is shared by the request and everything that happened inside it.  
*Figure: Application Insights Data Model — requests (incoming, id) → dependencies (outgoing, operation\_ParentId \= request id) and exceptions (operation\_ParentId \= request id); All Rows of One Operation Share operation\_Id*

| Table | One Row Is | Key Columns | Typical Question |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| requests | An incoming call to the app | name, resultCode, success, duration | How many calls failed, how slow were they? |
| dependencies | An outgoing call (SQL, HTTP, Redis) | target, type, name, resultCode, success, duration | Which downstream system is failing? |
| exceptions | An error thrown in the app | type, outerMessage, problemId | What error did the code see? |
| All three | Part of one operation | operation\_Id, operation\_ParentId, timestamp | What happened in this one user action? |

*Figure: KQL Pipeline — Table \| where (filter rows) \| extend (add columns) \| summarize … by (group) \| order / top \| render; join Matches Rows of Two Tables on operation\_Id*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Create an Application Insights resource and send telemetry to it from Cloud Shell  
* Filter and shape data with where, project and extend  
* Aggregate with summarize, count(), countif(), avg(), percentiles() and bin()  
* Visualise results with render timechart and columnchart  
* Identify and rank the top failing dependencies and separate benign failures  
* Correlate requests, dependencies and exceptions with join and operation\_Id

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER rank dependencies by failure count alone — check what the failures are (404 vs 503\) |
| ✗  NEVER join without a filter first — filter both sides to keep joins small |
| ✗  NEVER use the default join kind without knowing it — write kind=inner or kind=leftouter |
| ✗  NEVER send test telemetry into a production Application Insights resource — use your own |
| ✗  NEVER paste your connection string into a chat, ticket or file that is shared — treat it as a secret |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  KQL Is a Pipeline

A KQL query starts with a table and passes rows through operators: where keeps rows that match a condition, project chooses (and renames) columns, extend adds calculated columns, summarize groups rows and calculates aggregates (count(), countif(), avg(), percentiles(), dcount()), bin(timestamp, 1m) puts timestamps into buckets, order by / top sort, and render draws a chart. Operators run in the order written, so put where as early as possible. String comparison with \== is case-sensitive; \=\~ ignores case; has and contains search inside text.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| Every Azure monitoring tool — Application Insights, Log Analytics, Sentinel, Azure Resource Graph — uses KQL. A query you write here can become a workbook tile, a dashboard pin or a log search alert without rewriting. |
|  |
| Application Insights marks every HTTP dependency with a result code ≥ 400 as failed. That includes expected 404s, so the "most failed" dependency is often not the problem. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: requests vs dependencies vs exceptions

In workspace-based Application Insights the same tables are called AppRequests, AppDependencies and AppExceptions in the Log Analytics workspace, with other column names (for example DurationMs and Success); in the Logs blade of the Application Insights resource itself the classic names requests, dependencies and exceptions are still available, and this lab uses them. The success column can be returned as text in some schemas, so the queries compare tostring(success) \=\~ "false".

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With KQL |
| :---- |
| An engineer sorts dependencies by failure count, sees inventory-svc at the top and opens a ticket with the inventory team, while checkout payments keep failing. |
|  |
| REASON: inventory-svc returns 404 for unknown product IDs all hour — expected and harmless. The real incident is a smaller number of 503s and timeouts from the payment provider in a 15-minute window. |
|  |
| YOU MUST break failures down by resultCode and by time (bin()) and check which failures reach failed requests before you name a cause. |

## 3.3  join Kinds You Need

| Kind | Keeps | Example Use | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| innerunique (default) | Matches; left side de-duplicated by key | Rarely what you want | Surprising — always write kind= |
| inner | All matching pairs | Failed requests with their failed dependencies | Rows without a partner disappear |
| leftouter | All left rows, matches where they exist | Failed requests with exceptions, if any | Missing right side \= empty columns |
| union | Rows of several tables together | Timeline of one operation | withsource= names the source table |

| 📝  How to Decide Where a Failure Comes From |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do the failed requests share operation\_Id with failed dependencies, and what do the exceptions say?" If a failed request always has a failed call to one target and an exception from that client, that target is the cause. If a dependency fails but its requests fail with a 4xx that the client handles (404 → "product not found"), it is expected behaviour — record it and move on. |

| TASK 2 — SHAPE & AGGREGATE: where, project, extend, summarize, render |
| :---- |

| 2 | Filter, Shape and Aggregate Requests*Azure Application Insights SOP — Day 5 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

You use the core operators on the requests table: where and project to look at failed calls, summarize with count(), countif() and percentiles() to get the RED view per operation, and extend with case() and render to compare checkout before, during and after the incident.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Core operators (Application Insights → Logs) |
| :---- |
|  |
| // Step 1: where \+ project \+ take — what does a failed request look like? |
| requests |
| \| where tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| project timestamp, name, resultCode, duration, operation\_Id |
| \| take 5 ![][image11] |
| // Step 2: summarize — RED view per operation |
| requests |
| \| summarize calls \= count(), failed \= countif(tostring(success) \=\~ "false"), p50\_ms \= percentile(duration, 50), p95\_ms \= percentile(duration, 95\) by name |
| \| extend failed\_pct \= round(100.0 \* failed / calls, 1\) |
| \| order by failed desc ![][image12] |
| // Step 3: extend \+ case \+ render — checkout before / during / after (t0 \= first request of the hour) |
| let t0 \= toscalar(requests \| summarize min(timestamp)); |
| requests |
| \| where name \== "POST /api/checkout" |
| \| extend period \= case(timestamp \< t0 \+ 20m, "1-before", timestamp \< t0 \+ 35m, "2-during", "3-after") |
| \| summarize calls \= count(), failed \= countif(tostring(success) \=\~ "false"), avg\_ms \= round(avg(duration), 1), p95\_ms \= round(percentile(duration, 95), 0\) by period |
| \| order by period asc |
| \| render columnchart with (ycolumns \= failed) ![][image13] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 5 rows, e.g. GET /api/products/{id} 404 … and POST /api/checkout 502 … |
| Step 2: name calls failed p50\_ms p95\_ms failed\_pct |
| POST /api/checkout 367 52 ≈ 333 ≈ 5035 14.2 |
| GET /api/products/{id} 352 44 ≈ 23 ≈ 30 12.5 |
| GET /api/products 721 0 ≈ 31 ≈ 43 0 |
| GET /api/cart 261 0 ≈ 31 ≈ 43 0 |
| GET /health 99 0 ≈ 2 ≈ 3 0 |
| Step 3: 1-before 119 calls, 1 failed, avg ≈ 305 ms, p95 ≈ 420 · 2-during 83, 48 failed, avg ≈ 2523 ms, p95 ≈ 5052 · 3-after 165, 3 failed, avg ≈ 301 ms, p95 ≈ 421 |
| (KQL percentiles are estimates — values within a few ms are correct; Application Insights → Logs shows a table by default, use the Chart tab for the column chart) |
| **2.A  The products/{id} and checkout operations both fail 12–14 %. From Step 2 and 3, which one is an incident and why?**  : **Answer:** **`POST /api/checkout`** is an **incident**, whereas `GET /api/products/{id}` is not. **Why:** In Step 3, `POST /api/checkout` shows a sharp, temporary spike during the `2-during` window—failures jump to **48** (out of 83 calls), average duration rises to **\~2523 ms** (from \~305 ms before), and `p95` spikes to **\~5052 ms** (from \~420 ms before), before returning to normal (`~301 ms` avg, 3 failures) in `3-after`. By contrast, `GET /api/products/{id}` reflects steady/expected baseline behavior (such as routine 404 responses for non-existent IDs) rather than a time-bounded degradation.  |
| **2.B  What is the difference between where … \| summarize count() and summarize countif(…)?**  Answer: **`where <condition> | summarize count()`** filters the entire stream first so only matching rows remain, whereas **`summarize countif(<condition>)`** keeps all rows flowing through the pipeline and counts only those matching the condition—allowing you to compute conditional counts (and other metrics or breakdowns) in a single pass. **Why it matters in KQL:** Using `where ... | summarize count()` discards non-matching rows early, which is ideal when you only care about filtered events. Using `countif(...)` inside `summarize` lets you compare filtered counts alongside total calls or other aggregates (`calls = count(), failed = countif(...)`) in one query without running separate queries.   |

| TASK 3 — TOP FAILING DEPENDENCIES: Rank, Break Down, Time-Box |
| :---- |

| 3 | Identify the Top Failing Dependencies*Azure Application Insights SOP — Day 5 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

You rank dependencies by failures, break them down by target, type and resultCode, calculate the failure percentage and average duration per target, and draw failures over time to find the start and end of the payment-provider incident.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Failing dependencies (Application Insights → Logs) |
| :---- |
|  |
| // Step 1: top failing dependencies by target, type and result code |
| dependencies |
| \| where tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| summarize failed \= count() by target, type, resultCode |
| \| top 5 by failed desc ![][image14] |
| // Step 2: failure % and average duration per target |
| dependencies |
| \| summarize total \= count(), failed \= countif(tostring(success) \=\~ "false"), avg\_ms \= round(avg(duration), 1\) by target |
| \| extend failure\_pct \= round(100.0 \* failed / total, 1\) |
| \| order by failed desc ![][image15]  |
| // Step 3: when did the payment provider fail? |
| dependencies |
| \| where target \== "psp.example.com" and tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| summarize failures \= count() by bin(timestamp, 1m) |
| \| render timechart ![][image16] |
| // Step 4: first and last failure |
| dependencies |
| \| where target \== "psp.example.com" and tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| summarize first\_failure \= min(timestamp), last\_failure \= max(timestamp), failures \= count() ![][image17] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: inventory-svc HTTP 404 44 |
| psp.example.com HTTP (empty) 26 ← timeouts have no result code |
| psp.example.com HTTP 503 22 |
| sql-shop.database.windows.net \| shopdb SQL 1205 4 |
| Step 2: psp.example.com 363 / 48 / 773 ms / 13.2 % · inventory-svc 352 / 44 / 17.6 ms / 12.5 % |
| sql-shop… \| shopdb 1349 / 4 / 20.4 ms / 0.3 % · redis-shop.cache:6380 982 / 0 / 2.5 ms / 0 % |
| Step 3: bars only from minute 20 to minute 34 of the hour (1–7 failures per minute); zero before and after |
| Step 4: first \= 20 min after the start of your hour · last ≈ 14 min 56 s later · failures 48 (exact clock times depend on when you ran the script) |
| **3.A  List the top failing dependencies. Which is the incident, which is expected behaviour, and which is background noise?**  Answer: **Top failing dependencies:** psp.example.com (HTTP): **48** total failures (**26** with an empty resultCode from timeouts \+ **22** with HTTP 503), out of 363 calls (**13.2%** failure rate). inventory-svc (HTTP): **44** failures with HTTP 404, out of 352 calls (**12.5%** failure rate). sql-shop.database.windows.net \| shopdb (SQL): **4** failures with SQL code 1205, out of 1,349 calls (**0.3%** failure rate). **Classification: Incident:** psp.example.com (timeouts and 503 errors concentrated in minutes 20–34 of the hour, driving checkout failures). **Expected behaviour:** inventory-svc with HTTP 404 (routine not-found responses for requested product IDs). **Background noise:** sql-shop.database.windows.net \| shopdb with SQL 1205 (only 4 failures out of 1,349 calls, **0.3%**).  |
| **3.B  Why does psp.example.com have an average duration of ≈ 770 ms when its normal calls take ≈ 150–400 ms?**   Answer: The average duration (`avg(duration)`) is pulled upward by the **48 failed calls** (`26` timeouts \+ `22` `503` errors) during the incident window, which take much longer (such as multi-second timeouts or slow failed responses) than the normal `150–400 ms` successful calls.   |

# 

| TASK 4 — CORRELATE: join on operation\_Id, Exceptions, One Operation |
| :---- |

| 4 | Correlate Requests, Dependencies and Exceptions*Azure Application Insights SOP — Day 5 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

operation\_Id ties all telemetry of one user action together. You join failed requests with failed dependencies (inner join) and with exceptions (left outer join), and use union to show the full timeline of the first failed checkout.

| ⌨  Task 4 — Correlation (Logs, then Failures and End-to-end transaction) |
| :---- |
|  |
| // Step 1: failed requests → failed dependencies in the same operation |
| requests |
| \| where tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| project operation\_Id, name, resultCode |
| \| join kind=inner (dependencies \| where tostring(success) \=\~ "false" \| project operation\_Id, target, dep\_code \= resultCode) on operation\_Id |
| \| summarize count() by name, resultCode, target, dep\_code ![][image18]  |
| // Step 2: failed requests → exceptions (left outer: keep requests without exceptions) |
| requests |
| \| where tostring(success) \=\~ "false" |
| \| project operation\_Id, name, resultCode |
| \| join kind=leftouter (exceptions \| project operation\_Id, type) on operation\_Id |
| \| summarize count() by name, resultCode, type ![][image19]  |
| // Step 3: the first failed checkout, end to end |
| let op \= toscalar(requests \| where resultCode \== "502" \| top 1 by timestamp asc \| project operation\_Id); |
| union withsource=Table requests, dependencies, exceptions |
| \| where operation\_Id \== op |
| \| project timestamp, Table, name, target, resultCode, success, duration, type, outerMessage |
| \| order by timestamp asc ![][image20]  |
| // Step 4 (portal): Application Insights → Investigate → Failures → Operations tab → POST /api/checkout → "Drill into … samples" → pick one sample → End-to-end transaction details; then Investigate → Application map ![][image21] |
|  **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: POST /api/checkout 502 psp.example.com (empty) 26 |
| POST /api/checkout 502 psp.example.com 503 22 |
| POST /api/checkout 500 sql-shop… \| shopdb 1205 4 |
| GET /api/products/{id} 404 inventory-svc 404 44 |
| Step 2: checkout 502 PaymentTimeoutException 26 · checkout 502 PaymentProviderException 22 · checkout 500 SqlException 4 · products/{id} 404 (empty type) 44 |
| Step 3: 4 rows — request POST /api/checkout 502 false ≈ 625 ms · dependency INSERT shopdb 0 true ≈ 24 ms · dependency POST /v2/charges psp.example.com 503 false ≈ 586 ms · exception PaymentProviderException "PSP returned 503 Service Unavailable" |
| Step 4: Failures blade lists POST /api/checkout (52) and GET /api/products/{id} (44); the End-to-end transaction shows the same 4 items as a timeline; the Application map shows a red edge to psp.example.com |
| **4.A  Write the incident summary: cause, window, number of failed checkouts, evidence (the queries you used).**   Answer:   Cause: Payment provider (psp.example.com) failures—PaymentTimeoutException (26) and PaymentProviderException (22, e.g., 503 Service Unavailable on POST /v2/charges)—causing POST /api/checkout 502 errors (plus minor POST /api/checkout 500 / SqlException errors tied to shopdb). Window: 2-during incident window (t0 \+ 20m to t0 \+ 35m). Failed checkouts: 52 total failed POST /api/checkout calls (48 during 2-during, 1 before, 3 after). Evidence: Task 2 Step 2 & Step 3 (requests RED summary and 2-during checkout window); Task 4 Step 1 (inner join of failed requests and failed dependencies on operation\_Id), Step 2 (leftouter join of failed requests and exceptions on operation\_Id), Step 3 (union across requests, dependencies, and exceptions for the first 502 operation\_Id), and Step 4 (Failures blade and Application map).  |
| **4.B  Why do the 404 requests have no exception, and why did Step 2 need kind=leftouter to show them?**  Answer: A 404 response on GET /api/products/{id} from inventory-svc is a normal not-found response handled by the application rather than an unhandled runtime exception logged to the exceptions table. Step 2 needed kind=leftouter because a kind=inner join only returns operation\_Id rows present in both tables, whereas kind=leftouter keeps all failed requests from the left table and leaves type empty when no exception occurred.   |

# 

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| No rows in Logs | Telemetry not yet ingested, or wrong time range | Wait 2–5 minutes; time range Last 3 hours | Run the count query again; do not send the data twice |
| Script: "Set APPLICATIONINSIGHTS\_CONNECTION\_STRING first" | Variable missing in this Cloud Shell session | echo \$APPLICATIONINSIGHTS\_CONNECTION\_STRING | Export it again between single quotes (a new Cloud Shell session forgets it) |
| Script: HTTP 4xx or errors in the response | Connection string wrong, or local authentication disabled by policy | Overview → copy the connection string again; ask the instructor | Use your own resource; the instructor can allow ingestion by key or provide the shared resource |
| All counts doubled | Script ran twice | Run the row count query | Create a new resource with another name and send once |
| where success \== false returns nothing | success is stored as text in your schema | Run: requests \| getschema | Use tostring(success) \=\~ "false" as in this guide |
| join returns too many rows | Several rows per key on both sides | Count per operation\_Id | Filter first; summarize or use kind=inner deliberately |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — The Wrong Top Failure |
| :---- |
| inventory-svc was the top failing dependency. What would have happened if you had escalated it? |
| How would you stop 404s from being counted as failed in Application Insights? |
|  |
| Key insight: count is not impact — break down by resultCode and time; a telemetry processor can mark expected 404s as success. |
| **Discussion 2 — Timeouts Have No Code** |
| 26 PSP failures had an empty result code. What does that tell you? |
| How would a "group by resultCode" without them have changed your picture? |
|  |
| Key answer: timeouts never received a response — they show as empty codes and long durations (5000 ms). |
| **Discussion 3 — Join Kinds** |
| Why did Step 1 use inner and Step 2 leftouter? |
| What would the default innerunique have done in Step 2? |
|  |
| Answer: inner keeps only pairs; leftouter keeps requests without exceptions; innerunique de-duplicates the left side — always write the kind. |
| **Discussion 4 — From Query to Alert** |
| Which query from this lab would you turn into an alert, with which threshold? |
| Why alert on failed checkouts rather than on failed dependencies? |
|  |
| Key answer: alert on the user symptom (checkout failure rate); dependency queries are for diagnosis. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ranking by count only | Quick answer | Wrong team escalated | Break down by resultCode and time |
| Default join kind | Not written | Missing or de-duplicated rows | kind=inner / kind=leftouter |
| Joining unfiltered tables | Convenience | Slow queries, huge results | where before join |
| Text types for numbers | Default import | Comparisons fail | Explicit .create table schema |
| No incident window | Chart only | Vague report | min()/max() of failure timestamps |

# 8\. EXTENSION TASKS (Advanced Learners)

| Extension A — Dependency Latency Over Time |
| :---- |
| dependencies \| where target \== "psp.example.com" \| summarize percentiles(duration, 50, 95\) by bin(timestamp, 1m) \| render timechart |
| Describe what happened to successful PSP calls during the incident. (Run it against dependencies with the render timechart.) |
| Key question: would a latency alert have fired before the failures started?  `dependencies | where target == "psp.example.com" | summarize percentiles(duration, 50, 95) by bin(timestamp, 1m) | render timechart` *(If you want to isolate successful calls specifically, add `| where tostring(success) =~ "true"` before `summarize`.)* **What happened to successful PSP calls during the incident:** During the incident window (`2-during`, minutes `20–35` of the hour), PSP calls experienced sharp latency spikes (especially in `p95` duration) alongside timeouts and `503` failures on `POST /v2/charges`, before returning to normal baseline latency afterward. **Key question — Would a latency alert have fired before the failures started?** **No** (or only if latency rose ahead of failures without triggering a threshold earlier); latency spikes coincide with or follow the onset of dependency degradation rather than reliably giving an advance warning before failures start.  |
| **Extension B — Exceptions by problemId** |
| exceptions \| summarize count(), first \= min(timestamp), last \= max(timestamp) by problemId |
| Compare with the Failures blade of Application Insights. |
| Why does Application Insights group by problemId?  `exceptions | summarize count(), first = min(timestamp), last = max(timestamp) by problemId` **Compare with the Failures blade of Application Insights:** The KQL query gives exact per-`problemId` occurrence counts plus `first` and `last` timestamps in a table, whereas the **Failures** blade presents grouped error counts, top operations/exceptions visually, and one-click drill-down into end-to-end transactions. **Why Application Insights groups by `problemId`:** Grouping by `problemId` clusters similar exception occurrences (based on exception type, method/location, and error signature) so engineers can see the distinct root error groups and their first/last seen timestamps instead of getting flooded by individual event rows.  |
| **Extension C — Workspace Tables** |
| Open the Log Analytics workspace of your resource → Logs. |
| Run Task 3 Step 1 against the table AppDependencies. |
| Which column names change (Success, DurationMs, ResultCode, Target)? Open the **Log Analytics workspace** associated with your Application Insights resource, then go to **Logs**. Run Task 3 Step 1 adapted for the workspace schema (`AppDependencies`): Code snippet `AppDependencies | where tostring(Success) =~ "false" | summarize failed = count() by Target, DependencyType, ResultCode | top 5 by failed desc`  **Which column names change:** In workspace-based `AppDependencies` tables, PascalCase names are used instead of the classic Application Insights `dependencies` lowercase names—specifically **`Success`** (for `success`), **`DurationMs`** (for `duration`), **`ResultCode`** (for `resultCode`), and **`Target`** (for `target`) (along with `DependencyType` for `type`).  |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — APPLICATION INSIGHTS & KQL COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Filter | \| where success \== false and name has "checkout" | Rows |
| Choose columns | \| project timestamp, name, duration | Columns |
| Add column | \| extend pct \= round(100.0 \* a / b, 1\) | Calculated |
| Group | \| summarize count(), avg(duration) by name | Aggregates |
| Conditional count | countif(success \== false) | Failures |
| Percentiles | percentile(duration, 95\) · percentiles(duration, 50, 95\) | Latency |
| Time buckets | by bin(timestamp, 1m) | Time series |
| Chart | \| render timechart / columnchart | Visual |
| Rank | \| top 5 by failed desc | Top N |
| Join | \| join kind=inner (T2 \| project …) on operation\_Id | Correlate |
| Union | union withsource=Table requests, dependencies | Timeline |
| Variable | let op \= toscalar(…); | Reuse value |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — read once before class; learners do not need this section.  
1\. Subscription and rights: a sandbox subscription (never production). Each learner needs Contributor on their own resource group rg-shopai-\<seat\> (or Contributor on a shared resource group if names include the seat id) and the resource providers Microsoft.Insights and Microsoft.OperationalInsights registered. Cloud Shell needs a storage account for each learner the first time — create one shared storage account or allow Cloud Shell storage creation.  
2\. Ingestion by key: the script sends telemetry with the instrumentation key (connection string). If your organisation disables local authentication for Application Insights, ingestion by key is rejected. In that case use the shared option below, or switch the resource to allow it for the sandbox. This lab has not been run in your tenant — test with one seat before class.  
3\. Pre-class test: create one resource, run appinsights-gen.py, wait 5 minutes and confirm the numbers 1800 / 3046 / 52 and the queries of the guide. Check the expected values: failing checkout 52 (14.2 %), failing products/{id} 44 (12.5 %), PSP failures 48 starting 20 minutes after the start of the hour. If Logs returns success as text on your resource the queries still work (tostring(success)).  
4\. Pre-created option: appinsights-lab.arm.json (portal → Deploy a custom template → Build your own template in the editor → paste → Save) creates the workspace and the Application Insights resource for one seat; deploy it once per seat in a resource group named for the seat.  
5\. Shared option (no creation rights): create one Application Insights resource in the instructor subscription, run the script once, and give every learner the Reader role on it. Learners then open that resource → Logs and skip the resource creation and the script; all expected values stay the same. The resource must be loaded at least 15 minutes before class and the timestamps will be older than 10 minutes.  
6\. Cost and clean-up: about 4 MB of telemetry per learner, inside the 5 GB per month free allowance of Log Analytics; the workspace keeps data for 30 days by default. After class delete the resource groups rg-shopai-\<seat\> (Resource groups → select → Delete). Check the latest Azure Monitor pricing for your region.
